#6252. One of the world’s rarest fish lives in a single cave in Death Valley National Park, and earthquakes have left it on the verge of extinction

Devils Hole pupfish live in just one cavern of Death Valley National Park. Earthquakes are rapidly pushing this fish towards extinction.

One of the rarest fish on Earth lives in just one place: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert called Devils Hole, part of Death Valley National Park. In the spring of 2025, after two earthquakes shook its tiny home, biologists counted only 38 of them.

The National Park Service announced the new figure in November. Divers and surface counters found the 137 Devils Hole pupfish during a survey on October 10, nearly double the 77 seen in the spring of 2026 and about double the 69 recorded in the fall of 2025.

Devils Hole is a cave about 12 feet wide and more than 500 feet deep. The bottom has never been mapped. The water stays at a constant 92 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius).

Pupfish have been found as deep as 66 feet, but they feed and spawn only on a shallow rock shelf near the surface, where algae grows.

The species has been isolated there for 10,000 to 20,000 years, longer than any other pupfish in the Death Valley system. The region’s caves keep other long records too, like a Nevada cave that reveals 580,000 years of climate swings.

It is the only naturally occurring population of the species, which was listed as endangered in 1967. Biologists from the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service have counted the fish almost every spring and fall since 1972, with scuba divers in the cavern and counters at the surface.

One of the fish’s main threats can come from thousands of miles away. Large earthquakes as far away as Japan, Indonesia and Chile have made the water slosh in Devils Hole like water in a bathtub, according to the park.

Waves can splash as high as two meters (about 6.5 feet) up the walls and sweep the shelf clean. The park calls it a tsunami in the desert, although it is tiny next to the ocean tsunamis that big earthquakes can unleash.

That is what happened in the winter of 2024 to 2025. Two earthquakes, one in December and one in February, set off waves that moved algae, organic material and fish eggs off the shelf.

The spring count in 2025 found 38 fish. One year earlier, the official spring count had recorded 191.

On July 29, 2025, just 21 minutes after a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, waves rippled through Devils Hole, nearly 4,000 miles away. Those waves were only about 10 inches high and removed just some material from the shelf.

Then, after an earthquake in Panama on October 9, 2026, nearly 3,000 miles away, biologists at first saw signs of stress in the fish. On a later visit, they found them in healthier condition.

The team had prepared for a crash like this for years. Pupfish eggs from Devils Hole had been collected regularly to build a backup population at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility.

In 2025, biologists added captive-raised fish to the wild population for the first time. Between March 2025 and February 2026, scientists released 72 of them into Devils Hole. They also gave the fish extra food while the algae grew back.

The fish live an average of only 10 to 14 months. Because of that, biologists believe most of the 137 fish counted this fall hatched and grew up in Devils Hole itself.

“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” said Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds.

“These results reflect the dedication of our scientists and conservation partners working to protect this extraordinary species. While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival.”

The pupfish has survived human threats before. In the late 1960s, a farming operation drilled large wells in the Ash Meadows area, and the water level in Devils Hole began to drop toward the shelf the fish need.

Biologists even hung a floating, artificially lit shelf in the cave as a substitute. The fish never used it.

A federal court halted further pumping in 1971, and the fight reached the U.S. Supreme Court. Its 1976 decision in Cappaert v. United States recognized the water right of Devils Hole as part of a national monument and limited pumping so the natural shelf would stay underwater.

Until the mid-1990s, spring surveys counted more than 200 fish. In the early 2000s, spring counts averaged about 90, and in 2013 the number fell to 35. The cause of that long decline has not been determined.

The new count is an encouraging step, but the park says the population naturally fluctuates and remains highly vulnerable.

It calls continued monitoring, research and habitat management essential if one of the world’s rarest fish is to keep its foothold in a single desert cave.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s fall 2026 count announcement, its spring 2025 update, its report on the Kamchatka earthquake and its Devils Hole page.

#6251. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#6250. Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

Over 7,000 years, height rose and fell across Europe and Asia. Food quality, not tech, made the difference.

The dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

“When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”

To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

In China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

Trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan said. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

In Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

The authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

“Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” said Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, new, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”

Europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” said Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6249. What you just touched can change how the next thing feels

A study in rats found that frontal brain activity helped predict how an earlier vibration would bias judgments about the next one.

What you feel right now depends partly on what you felt a moment ago. In rats trained to judge vibrations, the primary sensory cortex mainly tracked the current vibration.

A region of the frontal cortex represented both the current and previous vibrations, and its activity helped predict how the previous vibration biased the rats’ judgments.

The study was carried out by neuroscientists at SISSA, the International School for Advanced Studies in Trieste, Italy.

“Perception is often thought of as a direct mapping of the external world,” explained Mathew Diamond, a cognitive neuroscientist at SISSA.

“Yet what we experience depends not only on what is happening now, but also on what happened moments ago. In short, every percept is constructed against a backdrop of recent experience.”

Scientists call this effect serial dependence, and it’s easy to picture. “Imagine feeling a vibration with your fingertip (for instance, from the cell phone) and then feeling a second vibration shortly afterward,” Diamond said.

“The second stimulus will not be experienced as an independent event; instead, perception is systematically biased by prior inputs. The brain, in effect, carries traces of the recent past into the present.”

“Perception is not a photograph of the world. It is more like a film, in which the experience of each frame is influenced by those that came before.”

Psychologists have known about the effect for a long time. Where the brain does the mixing, and how, has been much harder to work out.

Theories of “predictive processing” propose that the brain constantly combines incoming signals with expectations built from experience. What nobody had clearly shown was the neural machinery that brings the two together.

To find it, Diamond’s team trained rodents on a simple touch task. On each trial the animal felt a stimulus and had to decide whether it was weak or strong.

Meanwhile, the researchers recorded the activity of hundreds of neurons.

The animals’ judgments were consistently pulled by the previous trial. After a strong stimulus, the next one was more likely to be judged weak.

After a weak one, the next was more likely to be judged strong. A medium-strength touch could feel faint or firm depending on what had come right before it.

“The key finding emerged from comparing two cortical regions,” said lead author Iacopo Hachen.

“Activity in the primary sensory cortex mainly reflected the stimulus currently being processed, a direct representation of the ongoing input.”

“By contrast, neurons in a frontal cortical area carried information about both the current stimulus and recent sensory history. There, neural representations of the present were embedded within a context established by the past.”

The first stop for touch signals in the cortex, in other words, stayed true to the present. The frontal region carried the present and the recent past together.

The frontal region also helped predict the animals’ choices.

When its activity rose or fell from one trial to the next, the animals’ judgments shifted in step.

“Variations in this frontal-cortex activity predicted corresponding variations in perceptual judgments from one trial to the next, suggesting that while the sensory cortex faithfully reports the ongoing input, the frontal cortex integrates that input with recent experience to shape perception,” Hachen explained.

One region reports what is happening, and the other decides what it means given what just happened.

The researchers also identified a possible mechanism at the level of individual cells.

Fast-spiking neurons played a prominent role in how the frontal region represented both vibrations. Their firing patterns suggest they may be inhibitory neurons.

There was also an unexpected finding. While a touch was happening, the frontal neurons encoded it as an ongoing sensory event.

Once the animal committed to its answer, the code switched to a different, memory-like format. That stored version lasted and went on to bias the next decision.

In other words, the brain doesn’t just keep a recording of what happened. It rewrites the experience into a new format as it moves from perception into memory.

That rewritten trace then colors the next moment.

The authors see the work as evidence for a basic principle of how the brain works. Perception comes from a constant back-and-forth between new sensory evidence and traces of the recent past.

“Our findings suggest that the brain does not treat each moment in isolation. Instead, the recent past becomes part of the neural representation of the present, a unitary construct that mirrors our experience,” Hachen concluded.

Understanding this exchange could help explain how prediction normally supports behavior, and how it might go wrong in neurological and psychiatric disorders.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

#6248. Your home may be full of wildlife you’ve never noticed

A survey of indoor spaces across the U.S. and Canada recorded nearly 2,100 species, from familiar house spiders to an alligator in a garage.

Homes across the United States and Canada are full of wildlife.

A continent-wide survey has found nearly 2,100 species of wild organisms living indoors, mostly insects and spiders, plus centipedes, snails, fungi, and many animals most people have never heard of.

One record is an alligator that turned up in somebody’s garage.

This is the largest study of indoor wildlife so far. Nearly all of it is built from photos taken by ordinary people.

The study was led by researchers at North Carolina State University and Colorado State University.

Over 60 co-authors contributed, including museum curators, university entomologists, and independent experts from across North America and Europe.

Ecologists have spent decades cataloging life in rainforest canopies and on the deep sea floor. The places where most of us spend most of our time have received far less attention.

“While researchers have focused significant attention on a variety of natural ecosystems – from rainforest canopies to the deep sea – we know remarkably little about the ecosystems of manmade, indoor environments,” said lead author Bradley Allf from Colorado State.

“Our goal with this work was to treat the indoors, at the continental scale, as an ecosystem that we wanted to explore as ecologists,” he explained.

Earlier surveys of indoor life either covered much smaller areas or relied on DNA traces, which can’t always pin down exactly which species was present.

This is the first survey of indoor life spanning the United States and Canada.

The team launched a citizen science project called Never Home Alone on iNaturalist, a website where people share photos of the living things they come across.

Participants were asked to photograph wild organisms in their homes, offices, and other indoor spaces. The rule for “wild” was simple: anything that was neither a pet nor a potted plant.

Submissions came from at least five continents. This study focuses on North America.

About 3,000 people contributed 23,782 observations, from every US state and every Canadian province. Most were taken in homes, but some came from offices, schools, and airports. The records cover almost three decades, from 1996 to 2024.

Every observation was checked by specialists. Dozens of experts identified each organism as precisely as they could.

“This work underscores the value of natural history expertise and the ability to identify species, which is a skillset that is less common among biologists than it once was,” Allf said.

About 95% of the observations were arthropods, the group of animals with jointed legs and hard outer skeletons. Insects made up 60% of all records, mostly beetles, flies, moths, wasps and ants, and true bugs.

Spiders accounted for 30%. Animals with backbones made up only 4%, most of them reptiles and mammals.

The rest included fungi, plants, earthworms, snails, small crustaceans, and even single-celled organisms.

Eight species were recorded more than 200 times each.

In order, they were the Asian lady beetle, the brown marmorated stink bug, the house centipede, the varied carpet beetle, the long-bodied cellar spider, the triangulate combfoot spider, the bathroom moth fly, and the eastern parson spider.

“The organisms we found ranged from Asian lady beetles – which were the most commonly found species – to an alligator that unexpectedly turned up in one person’s garage,” Allf said.

“But one of the things that was striking was how common predator species were – including hundreds of different spider species.”

Half of the top eight are hunters, and some of them do useful work.

“One study participant noted that they view jumping spiders as working animals, because the spiders play an active role in reducing the population of flies and other pests that they don’t want in their home.”

Senior author Rob Dunn from NC State pointed out that most people share their homes with these animals every day and have no idea what they are.

“Another thing that is striking about this work is that most people could look over a list of the most commonly found species and wouldn’t know what most of those animals even are – and yet they are around us, all the time,” he said.

“For example, I suspect most people are unfamiliar with comb-footed spiders, but we have more than a thousand observations of this family of spiders.”

“This is a stark departure from what we would have expected historically, when our ancestors would have been more aware of the living things around them.”

“That’s something we lost. And this is a first step toward regaining that understanding.”

The list has a very long tail. About 52% of the species were recorded indoors just once.

The true total is almost certainly higher than 2,100, because 44% of the observations couldn’t be identified down to species.

The authors also point out the dataset’s limits. Nobody controlled how hard each person looked, so large, eye-catching animals are probably overrepresented.

And not every animal that ends up indoors actually lives there. Some had simply wandered in and become trapped.

The survey also shows how little is known about even the most common indoor animals.

“It could inform future research in many ways,” Dunn said.

“For example, house centipedes were the third most commonly found animals, and yet I’m not aware of anyone who is studying them. That’s worth exploring.”

Some of these animals might even turn out to be useful.

“For example, we now know that camel crickets carry a microbe that can break down paper products. That could be useful. What else might be out there, in our own homes?”

“Once we know what’s there, we can begin asking additional questions,” Dunn said.

“Why are these organisms there? What are they doing? Are they beneficial?”

“But knowing what’s there is the first step. And it’s exciting because these are the animals we’re around all the time, but we just overlook.”

The scientists want to investigate how the climate outside shapes what turns up inside. They also plan to figure out which species have actually adapted to life in buildings.

Every record has a date and a location, so the dataset can also serve as a baseline for spotting new arrivals or disappearances in the future. The data are free for anyone to use.

The project is still running, and anyone with a phone can contribute.

“People can still submit observations to Never Home Alone. The more data the project collects, the more insight we’ll have on the unique and growing ecosystem of the great indoors,” Allf concluded.

The study is published in the journal Ecology.

#6247. This year’s El Niño is unlike any other on record

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

El Niño’s hallmark tongue of warm water extends thousands of kilometers from South America's Pacific coast. This map from November 14 shows the tongue’s average surface temperature was at least 3 degrees Celsius (dark red) above normal.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the New Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#6246. The 6 Best Smart Thermostats to Keep Your House Comfortable and Save You Money

Get more efficient heating and cooling with these set-it-and-forget-it models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience. In this case, it’s your temperature controls. These devices tend to be a bit pricier than conventional thermostats, but it’s an upgrade that can pay for itself over time thanks to increased energy efficiency.

Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely. That comes in handy when, let’s say, you want to warm up the house earlier than usual if you head home from work early. You’re also able to track your usage with monthly energy reports, which can help you bring down your bills.

For the past few months, my colleagues and I have been steadily testing smart thermostats throughout in our homes, including models from Google Nest, ecobee, and Honeywell Home. These are the models we tried, plus a few more we recommend based on our research and reviews. We’ve also included some expert advice on what to consider before you buy.

The ecobee covers the standard lineup of smart thermostat features, with climate control and money-saving that are commonplace among any of the top options, but sets itself apart with a wider range of smart features.

It doubles as a security base for your home security, serving as the arming and disarming mechanism. It also features a built-in air quality monitor that alerts you to poor air quality and sends reminders when you need to replace air filters in your furnace.

The ecobee comes with a separate smart sensor for precision control, allowing it to fine-tune the temperature in the rooms where you spend the most time. Though it comes with a single sensor, you can purchase more to add that precision throughout the house.

It also provides free Eco+ Software which works on your smartphone and generates energy reports that further maximize your energy savings.

The smart thermostat also comes with a host of standard smart features. After connecting to a Google assistant or Alexa, the smart speaker built directly on the thermostat itself can take voice commands and even play music. It also comes with a three-year warranty from date of purchase.

Each purchase comes with a full converter kit as well, so if you aren’t currently in a home with a C-Wire, you can add one by following the kit instructions.

For a smart thermostat that better fits a tight budget, Amazon has its own option that comes with many of the same energy-saving features at a lower overall price tag. Through the connected app, the thermostat tracks and reports your energy usage and peak time periods throughout the week and month.

Through Alexa, you can also set home, away, and sleep temperatures that you can schedule throughout the day and week in order to further maximize savings on your energy bill and optimize your air conditioning to your exact schedule. You can also set the temperature remotely from your phone through the Alexa app.

Beyond the controls, by using an Amazon product, the company will pass along potential rebate and saving opportunities that you could take advantage of by owning a smart thermostat.

As for upfront costs, the device is designed specifically for easy DIY installation so there is no need to hire an HVAC technician unless you want one.

The Honeywell T9 is a great choice if your primary concern is reducing energy use and lowering your bills. You need to pair it with one of Honeywell’s smart room sensors to take advantage of the thermostat’s full functionality, which is an extra hurdle, but the sensor only costs about $30, so it’s a short one.

One of the key ways the T9 saves money is through virtual fencing. Using your phone’s GPS, the thermostat automatically switches between home and away mode as you come and go. So, when you leave your house, energy usage is reduced across the board.

Honeywell also provides monthly usage reports that point out areas where energy can be reduced for a lower upfront cost. Adding more room sensors can increase the accuracy of those reports, giving you more chances to optimize your heating and cooling system.

The Honeywell T9 doesn’t have the same wide spectrum of features as our other recommendations, but it’s core functionality is very solid.

The newest generation of the Google Nest Thermostat has impressed our team as an easy-to-install, easy-to-use option that reduces energy use and is compatible with most HVAC systems. Like previous models, the smart thermostat builds a schedule, learns your temperature preferences, and reduces energy when it isn’t needed.

Reviews Editor Danny Perez installed the Nest in his own home and absolutely fell in the love with nearly every aspect of it. “To say I like this thermostat is an understatement: It lights up when I pass by to show me the interior temps, as well as local weather and humidity (it’s nice to know my presence is acknowledged, not gonna lie),” writes Perez.

Beyond the basic features, Perez also pointed out how much he likes the actual display and design of the thermostat. “Sure, other thermostats and window a/c units have similar smart features, but they don’t blend into my home the way the Google Nest thermostat does. I genuinely enjoy looking at it. I light up when I pass by it.”

With a large, responsive touch screen, this basic Honeywell thermostat is easy to see from across the room, thanks to a large, custom-color display. It’s a versatile option, compatible with multiple smart home assistants. Like other models, it’s Energy Star-certified, which means that using one can help you save even more money through local rebates.

While the smart thermostat is great for easy scheduling and reading, it lacks the learning software of the Google Nest or the virtual fencing adjustments that many other smart thermostats have. That said, it’s also considerably cheaper.

Most smart thermostats aren’t compatible with baseboard heating and cooling systems. This Mysa unit is the rare exception, and designed specifically to work with electric baseboards. Combine that with compatibility across every major smart home system, and the Mysa becomes one of very few thermostats with such capabilities.

While the compatibility alone makes this a tempting choice, it also has many of the same high-end smart features as the competition. This includes virtual fencing, so when you head out for the day, the thermostat automatically reduces energy use.

Another key feature is its temperature monitor. Unlike many other devices, which only provide you with degrees, the Mysa smart thermostat also measures and reports humidity levels.

Traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential issue you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

If this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

Some smart thermostats include installation kits that provide equipment and step-by-step instructions for adding a C-Wire to your current wiring. This can be a helpful addition to the handier among us, and may circumvent the need for an HVAC technician entirely, though you may want to keep one waiting in the wings if anything goes wrong.

Once you've wired and installed your smart thermostat, you can connect it to other devices in your home via Wi-Fi or occasionally Z-Wave. Most units are compatible with many major smart home ecosystems. While they’re compatible with many systems, I would still take a moment to check and make sure that a thermostat works specifically with the smart home setup you use at home.

Along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

Several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

They’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. More precise temperature control also increases the potential for saving energy. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

The Popular Mechanics Gear Team has tested several of these recommendations over the course of several months, including the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium and the Google Nest Learning Thermostat. We installed these smart thermostats in our homes, set them up, and used them to keep ourselves warm and cool, as the seasons demanded. We gave them our seal of approval based on ease-of-use, installation process, programmable features, and how well the devices integrated with our smart home assistants, mobile devices, and tablets.

A few thermostats, such as the Honeywell Home Smart Color Thermostat, made the list despite the fact that we haven’t tested them yet. In those cases, we picked options from established brands with the specs and features that are comparable to our tested recommendations, and have received strong reviews from customers at online retailers.

We also prioritized options that were highly compatible with other smart devices and offered convenient features for everyday use. Price rice was a major consideration, as well: We chose models ranging from roughly $160 to $250, ensuring that we recommend a range of options that fit every need and budget.

#6245. In a West Texas rock shelter, archaeologists found a hunting kit that was left behind 6,500 years

Archaeologists in Texas uncovered a roughly 6,500-year-old hunting kit with darts, an atlatl and a rare preserved pronghorn hide.

Deep inside San Esteban Rockshelter, south of Marfa, Texas, archaeologists recovered parts of a hunter’s weapon kit that someone left behind thousands of years ago.

The Center for Big Bend Studies at Sul Ross State University presented the find in its spring 2025 newsletter. The center puts the kit’s age at about 6,500 years and calls it “potentially the oldest example of a full weapon system in North America.”

The kit as a whole has not yet been described in a peer-reviewed study. Only one of its pieces, a spear-thrower known as an atlatl, has been the subject of a journal paper.

The kit includes six stone-tipped dart foreshafts – the front section of a dart – and four self-tipped hardwood dart foreshafts

There are also four dart nock-ends, the rear tips that fit against the atlatl. A broken hunting boomerang and a partial atlatl complete the weapons.

The excavators also found a folded pronghorn hide. It had been tanned, and its hair was still intact.

Spaced holes ran around the hide’s perimeter so it could be tied to a frame, as Plains groups often did.

“We just sat there and stared at it in wonder,” said Bryon Schroeder, then director of the center. Someone had folded the hide and set it on top of a rock, he explained.

“And nobody touched it for 6,000 years,” Schroeder said.

An atlatl is essentially a wooden stick with a handle on one end and a hook or socket on the other. It acts as an extension of the human arm, increasing leverage against the dart, the National Park Service explains.

The San Esteban atlatl is described in a 2023 atlatl paper by Schroeder and Devin Pettigrew, an assistant professor at the center.

A radiocarbon date indicates that the atlatl is more than 6,000 years old. That made it the oldest directly dated atlatl in North America at the time, the authors reported in the Journal of Big Bend Studies.

In a paper published in 2026, Pettigrew and other archaeologists at the center measured how fast modern throwers launch darts.

That research shows that heavier darts, paired with strong and skilled throwers, become lethal to very large animals such as mammoths, the center said.

“In most archeological sites in Texas, only things made of stone survive,” notes Texas Beyond History, a project of the University of Texas at Austin. The dry Lower Pecos rock shelters are an exception.

Those shelters have yielded hardwood dart foreshafts and rabbit sticks, as well as bow fragments and arrow foreshafts from the bow-and-arrow era. Complete atlatls are very rare even there.

Unique depositional conditions favored the preservation of the Schöningen wooden spears in Germany. A 2025 dating study placed them at about 200,000 years old.

A mammoth-ivory boomerang from Poland is one of the oldest known in Europe, an Obłazowa Cave analysis concluded. A statistical model built on dated bones from the same layer places it between 42,290 and 39,280 years ago.

“We can use the wood to reconstruct the environment and learn more about the amount of time they spent working on tools,” Schroeder said.

Schroeder’s reading of the scene is that a person came to the back of the cave and sorted through the gear piece by piece. Some parts were judged good and others not, and then the person went on their way.

“But that one small act is going to have profound implications in understanding the environment,” he said.

The shelter sits in Presidio County along Alamito Creek, a tributary of the Rio Grande. A spring-fed rock pool, or tinaja, lies in front of it.

The center has worked there since 2019 with the Odyssey Archaeological Research Fund at the University of Kansas. The partners were looking for traces of the region’s earliest people.

The Odyssey fund was established in 2003 with an endowment from Joseph and Ruth Cramer. Its director is Rolfe Mandel, a distinguished professor of anthropology at the university.

In 2020, the excavators uncovered a hearth-like feature with burned and unburned bird eggshells dated to about 15,200 years ago.

“Though this site was pot-hunted in the past, the many large boulders that spalled from the ceiling preserved pockets of shelter deposits,” the Kansas team’s site summary states. Pot-hunting means digging for artifacts to collect.

The atlatl foreshafts and darts came from intact deposits in an area the excavators call the Sandal Shaft. The Kansas team dates them to about 6,200 years ago, a little younger than the center’s figure.

The pronghorn hide lay about 2 inches (5 centimeters) above them, capped with a metate, a grinding stone.

The hide yielded a raw radiocarbon age of 5,621 years, plus or minus 24, not yet converted to calendar years. That makes it about 600 years younger than some of the foreshafts and darts, the Kansas researchers report.

The information was obtained from the Center for Big Bend Studies.

#6244. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

Chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”

Astronomers once assumed galaxies were born before black holes, but giant black holes spotted in the early universe are forcing them to rethink their order of events.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly every large galaxy is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its center. The Milky Way's black hole, known as Sagittarius A*, is enormous, weighing over 4 million times as much as the sun. But which came first: the black holes or the galaxies around them?

Astronomers told Live Science that they thought they knew, but new observations mean they're no longer sure.

For decades, the prevailing idea was that galaxies came first: Dying massive stars leave behind black holes that can merge and feed until they swell to millions of times the sun's mass, said Joseph Silk, an astrophysicist and professor at Johns Hopkins University.

Then, in recent years, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) began peering back at the early universe. "Recent observations are challenging this picture, or at least showing us that it cannot be the whole story," Roberto Maiolino, a professor of astrophysics at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science in an email. "We are finding extremely massive black holes just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang."

The galaxy GHZ2 (white box) contains the oldest known supermassive black hole. Discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, its light had to travel some 13.4 billion years to reach Earth.

Stranger still, some of these black holes look too big for their hosts. In nearby galaxies, a central black hole is typically about a thousand times less massive than its galaxy, Maiolino said, but some early ones "appear to be almost as massive as the stars in their host galaxies." In a study in the journal Nature, Maiolino and colleagues measured one such black hole's mass directly in an object called Abell2744-QSO1 and found that it holds most of the object's mass.

So where could such giants come from? Maiolino outlined several possibilities, and more than one may be correct. Some supermassive black holes may be ordinary stellar remnants that grew much faster than usual. Others may have been "born big," forming from the direct collapses of enormous gas clouds, which "would give the black hole a head start in its growth," Maiolino explained. Another idea is that these monsters were seeded by primordial black holes that formed "shortly after the Big Bang, before the first stars and galaxies existed."

Further complicating the question is that black holes and galaxies also push and pull on each other. A growing black hole can release an enormous amount of energy that heats or expels gas, which, in turn, curbs or shuts down star formation, Maiolino said.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

However, it can also compress gas and potentially trigger new stars. "Black holes and galaxies influence one another throughout their evolution, and neither can be understood entirely in isolation," he said.

A black hole spewing jets inside the elliptical galaxy Centaurus A.

Silk said the balance varies. In giant, elliptical galaxies, black holes weighing billions of suns can have "histories of extreme violence" that helped limit their hosts' growth, while in spirals like the Milky Way, feedback from stars tends to dominate.

So which came first? Answering that question will take far more data from JWST. Right now, "we have samples of tens of objects, maybe 20, 30, 40," Silk said, and astronomers need far more data to tell whether oversize black holes are typical.

If black holes outweigh their galaxies the farther back astronomers look, that would strongly suggest black holes formed first, Silk said; if stars dominate, it would point the other way.

Maiolino suggested the question itself may need rethinking. "Asking which came first may be too simplistic," he said. "The more interesting question may be how black holes and galaxies formed, grew and influenced one another at different stages of cosmic history."

There may be no single sequence. "Different black holes, in different environments and at different cosmic epochs, may have formed and evolved through different pathways," Maiolino added.

For now, the cosmic chicken-and-egg puzzle remains open. As Maiolino put it, astronomers are "beginning to explore a period of cosmic history for which we still have many unanswered questions."

#6242. Flightless kākāpō parrots from New Zealand are genetically healthy despite 10,000 years of inbreeding

Scientists sequenced the DNA of New Zealand's endangered kākāpō and found that 10,000 years of inbreeding actually helped natural selection clear out harmful genetic mutations.

On New Zealand’s Stewart Island, flightless parrots called kākāpō spent about 10,000 years cut off from the rest of their species, breeding with relatives. In theory, that should have left the birds with more and more harmful mutations.

A 2021 study of their DNA found the opposite: the island kākāpō carried fewer harmful mutations than mainland kākāpō, which have since died out.

The researchers wrote that the finding is evidence a small population can survive hundreds of generations of isolation. The species is still critically endangered, though, and many of its eggs fail to hatch.

Nicolas Dussex, a researcher at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, led the study. Few birds anywhere are as inbred or as endangered as the kākāpō, Dussex said.

Kākāpō likely numbered in the hundreds of thousands before people reached New Zealand. Overhunting and predators introduced by people reduced them to 51 birds by 1995.

Fifty came from Stewart Island. The other was a mainland male named Richard Henry.

When the study came out, 201 kākāpō were alive, all on island sanctuaries.

For 49 kākāpō, Dussex’s team analyzed each bird’s complete set of DNA, called its genome. Thirty-five were Stewart Island birds.

The rest were mainland birds: Richard Henry and 13 museum specimens. Those specimens were collected between 1847 and 1924.

An inbred bird’s DNA has a recognizable pattern. A chick gets one copy of its genome from each parent. When the parents are related, long stretches of the two copies match.

In the Stewart Island birds, matching stretches made up 53% of the genome on average. In the mainland birds, matching stretches made up 15%.

So the island birds were far more inbred. The team then counted the most damaging kind of mutation, the kind predicted to stop a gene from working.

Mainland birds carried 34.1 of those mutations on average. Island birds carried 17.6 of them, about half as many.

Many of these mutations seem to do harm mainly when a bird inherits the same one from both parents. That happens more often when the parents are related.

Chicks that inherit the mutation from both parents are less likely to survive or breed, the team suggested. Over many generations, the mutation becomes rarer. Geneticists call that process purging.

The team tested the idea with computer simulations spanning 25,000 years. A simulated population that stayed small, like Stewart Island’s, ended up with fewer harmful mutations than a larger one like the mainland’s.

But in a simulated population one-tenth as large as the island’s, the harm from mutations grew instead. So purging seems to need enough birds for natural selection to work.

After the kākāpō’s recent decline, the team wrote, the birds may now face the same growing harm as that smallest population.

Conservation managers have favored matings with Richard Henry and his offspring, to help the population keep its ability to adapt.

“We show that the single male survivor from the mainland, Richard Henry, has more harmful mutations than Stewart Island birds,” said Love Dalén of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, who supervised the study.

“Therefore, there could be a risk that these harmful mutations spread in future generations.”

Richard Henry was also genetically distinct, Dalén added, and may have carried useful genetic diversity. The team recommended weighing that benefit against the risk and, if necessary, limiting breeding between the two family lines.

Dussex’s team counted mutations in DNA and didn’t measure what they do to a living bird. Their effects on survival and breeding weren’t known.

The team called for research into the genetic causes of the kākāpō’s low fertility and hatching success.

In some other shrinking species, harmful mutations increased as numbers fell, the authors wrote. In others, the mutations decreased.

Next, the team planned to examine other highly inbred birds and mammals, to learn whether the kākāpō is a rare exception.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Genomics.

#6241. The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

He has good reason to believe this marvel of ancient Rome may surpass all modern concrete methods.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

For decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he says he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

Scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

But it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

Then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first big clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic says. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

Masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

The research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic says. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

The team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

Roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less new material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

Our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, says Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In fact, Masic co-founded a company in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also plans to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6240. Growing mountain ranges played a major role in sparking life on Earth

Rocks once buried in mountain belts suggest Earth's ranges grew taller in two steps, each near a rise in oxygen and in complex life.

Picture the young Earth and you probably see mountains in your mind. For the planet’s first billion years or more, it may not have had any that would resemble the majestic mountain ranges our planet has today.

Rocks that were once buried deep inside mountain ranges suggest the ranges grew taller in two steps, a new study finds. The first step ended about 2.2 billion years ago and the second about 700 million years ago.

Each step came around the time Earth’s air gained oxygen and life grew more complex.

Matthijs Smit, an associate professor of earth sciences at the University of British Columbia, led the work.

The link to life is a match in timing, not a demonstrated cause. The authors call it a hypothesis that still has to be tested.

When two plates collide, rock gets shoved downward as well as up. Minerals that form under that squeeze keep a record of the pressure they felt, and pressure translates into depth.

The deepest-buried rocks that later return to the surface mark roughly how thick a mountain belt’s crust had grown. Smit’s team gathered pressure and age estimates for such rocks from around the world.

The team relied on garnet, a mineral that forms during the burial itself and can be dated precisely. They also added new measurements from ancient rocks in Cameroon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In an interview with Earth.com, Smit said the debate over the early Earth has run between two pictures.

“Some would argue that it was an almost alien world, with no emerged lands, whereas others would argue that it operated very much in the same way as the modern Earth, with large mountain chains, active tectonics and widespread emerged lands,” he said.

Before about 2.7 billion years ago, the rocks record burial no deeper than roughly 19 to 22 miles (30 to 35 kilometers). In the long middle era that followed, mountain belts buried rock to 34 to 37 miles (55 to 60 kilometers).

The middle-era depth is roughly double the earlier one. In the current era, rocks have come back from about 56 miles (90 kilometers) down, about half again as deep.

The modern figure matches the crust under the Himalaya and Pamir today.

What surprised Smit was how steady the maximum depth stayed within each era, and how consistently it changed from one era to the next.

“There does seem to be a specific tectonic style for each episode in the tectonic evolution of the lithosphere, which dictates in a broad sense how thick (and tall) mountains could become,” he said.

Thicker crust generally stands higher above sea level. Using the relationship between thickness, density, and elevation seen today, the team converted the depths into rough heights.

Before 3 billion years ago, the highest terrain comes out at sea level, within the error bars. Through the middle era, the highest peaks could have stood about 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) tall, roughly half the height of Everest.

Mountains of that era were real, then, but they were not the giants of today.

For the modern era, the method gives about 5.5 miles (8.8 kilometers). That is the height of Everest, K2, and Kangchenjunga, to within the uncertainty.

The authors note the sea-level comparison holds for recent geological time and probably for the middle era too. In the earliest era, the oceans were larger and the crust denser, so those early heights are rougher guesses.

Most of the sediment that rivers carry to the sea comes from mountains, and the amount depends on erosion above about 1.9 miles (3 kilometers) of altitude.

Taller mountains mean more rock washed into the oceans, and with it phosphorus, which limits how much marine life can grow.

Both growth periods line up, broadly, with the two great rises in atmospheric oxygen. Each oxygen rise was followed by a Snowball Earth ice age and then by a jump in the amount and variety of life.

Strontium in ancient seawater, which tracks how much material was coming off the continents, also rose during both periods. Phosphorus would have behaved the same way, the authors argue, because it is held in similar minerals.

“It’s likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,” said co-author Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History.

The match isn’t perfect, and the authors say so. Some records of oxygen and living matter don’t move in step with the mountains. That could mean the hypothesis is wrong, or that the planet responded to extra nutrients in thresholds and delays.

Why would mountains grow taller only at certain times? “We suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,” Smit said. “As a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.”

In the authors’ reading, the first change was the arrival of plate tectonics as we know it, with one plate sliding beneath another and crust piling up.

The second came as the cooling mantle let continental margins be dragged deeper before snapping free. That is how the thickest mountain belts are built today.

Old, deeply buried rocks rarely survive. Such rocks are the most likely to be altered by later events or lost back into the mantle, so the record is thinnest exactly where the first step happened.

Smit told Earth.com that the first change is pinned down only to a window of several hundred million years, ending around 2 billion years ago.

“We don’t know precisely how this change occurred in time and whether it was even one continuous change or whether there were short bursts by which mountains were able to get higher and higher,” he said.

Until that window narrows, the timing can’t be checked closely against the changes in the oceans and atmosphere, Smit said.

That work starts with more field research in ancient terrains, sampling rocks and measuring their pressures and ages. He also suggested Earth system models that include step-like, tectonically driven increases in phosphorus.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances. Co-authors are at Utrecht University, the Swedish Museum of Natural History, and the Geological Survey of Canada, among others.

#6239. How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Sebnem Ece Eksi wants to see how nerves change as cancer progresses. She hopes those changes could offer clues for detecting tumors earlier.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”

Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”

#6238. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6237. In 1966, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies, and photos from Gemini flights like his helped inspire the revolutionary Landsat satellites

Sixty years ago, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies on Gemini XII. NASA says Gemini photos also helped make the case for satellites like Landsat.

Sixty years ago this month, Buzz Aldrin opened the hatch of his Gemini spacecraft, looked outside and exclaimed, “Man! Look at that!”

Near the end of that spacewalk, on November 12, 1966, he mounted a camera on the edge of the hatch, pointed it at himself and took the first selfies ever taken during a spacewalk. NASA notes that it happened decades before the concept even existed.

That flight, Gemini XII, is better known for something else. It finally showed that astronauts could do useful work outside a spacecraft, a skill NASA needed before it could send anyone to the Moon.

And a NASA image article published on November 13 points to a quieter legacy: photos like the ones Aldrin and his commander took from orbit helped inspire the program that led to the Landsat satellites.

Aldrin and command pilot James A. Lovell launched on November 11, 1966, on a four-day mission. It was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini program, which had to prove the techniques that Apollo would need to land on the Moon.

Those techniques included rendezvous and docking, spacewalking, and showing that spacecraft and astronauts could function for at least eight days, the minimum for a round trip to the Moon.

Spacewalks were the weak spot. Astronauts on the Gemini IX, X and XI missions had run into significant difficulties outside their spacecraft, and NASA looked for better ways to train.

On September 12, 1966, Aldrin became the first astronaut to train for his spacewalks underwater, using mockups of the Gemini and its target vehicle in a school swimming pool in Owings Mills, Maryland. Neutral buoyancy training, as it is called, is still in use today.

Gemini XII launched about 90 minutes after an uncrewed Agena target vehicle. When the crew’s rendezvous radar proved erratic, Aldrin used backup methods and onboard calculations to guide them in.

He had written his doctoral dissertation on orbital rendezvous. They docked on the third orbit.

A problem with the Agena’s engine stopped a planned boost to a higher orbit. Instead, Mission Control told the crew that a slight change would put them on the path of a solar eclipse the next morning.

On November 12, as they flew over the Galapagos Islands, the nearly total eclipse came into view, and Aldrin took several photographs and a short film clip.

It was the first time a solar eclipse was photographed from Earth orbit, according to NASA. Gemini XII passed within 3.4 miles of the center of the eclipse’s path.

Later that day, Aldrin made his first spacewalk, a “standup” outing in which he stayed in the open hatch. He installed a handrail on the Agena for the next day, photographed stars in ultraviolet light and took his selfies. He spent two hours and 28 minutes outside.

The next day, tied to the spacecraft by a 30-foot umbilical, he moved along the handrail to the Agena and later worked at the back of the Gemini with his feet in restraints called “golden slippers.”

He completed 19 tasks in all, reporting no problems with keeping his body in position. At two hours and nine minutes, it was the longest umbilical spacewalk to that time.

A third standup spacewalk brought his total to a then-record five hours and 48 minutes. Aldrin credited his underwater training and adequate restraint systems for his success.

Spacewalks have come a long way since then: in September 2024, the crew of SpaceX’s Polaris Dawn mission carried out the first civilian spacewalk.

On November 14, 1966, Lovell and Aldrin also photographed the area around the Red Sea and the Nile River valley. NASA featured that image in its November 13 article.

According to the agency, the photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface, and helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program.

One of the strongest advocates for Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, director of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from 1965 to 1971.

In a 1969 statement, he said the Earth Resources Observation Satellite program he championed, which later paved the way for Landsat, was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.”

For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have been used to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health and land use. In October, Landsat 9 captured autumn’s colors in the forests around Ripton, Vermont.

Lovell and Aldrin splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean on November 15, 1966, only three miles from the planned target. The flight lasted 94 hours and 34 minutes.

Gemini flew 10 crewed missions in 20 months, and all of the program’s major objectives were accomplished. Less than three years later, Aldrin walked on the Moon with Apollo 11. The Gemini XII spacecraft is on display at the Adler Planetarium in Chicago.

The information was obtained from NASA’s history of the Gemini XII mission, its account of eclipses seen from space and its image article on Gemini Earth photography.
