#6070. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

Our four-year-old is currently at the age where he asks “why” in response to everything… and he has a lot of good questions that often make me step back and think “oh, that’s a good point.” I put myself in the situation of being on the jet bridge here as a parent, and trying to explain what was going on.

And here’s the thing — it’s one thing if these people were in uniform and identifying themselves, but when you have people who refuse to identify themselves, it’s an especially bad look. It reminds me of another incident we recently saw at Las Vegas Airport (LAS). Like, is this person being robbed in the terminal, or is this an official law enforcement operation?

A post shared by Chris Motley (@motleymodel)

On Saturday, an Alaska Airlines flight was delayed by a few hours after ICE agents stormed a jet bridge to arrest someone, leading to a larger fight, which also caused more arrests. It’s one thing if such a disruptive operation were targeting a violent criminal, but is this really the way that someone who overstays a visa should be apprehended?

The Port of Seattle has expressed outrage over how this was handled, while ICE is outraged at how its “brave law enforcement” is facing increasing violence from the public.

Delay flight by 3 hours, arrest several people and traumatise even more. Sounds like a proportionate response to catching one person that overstayed their visa.

I find it interesting that enforcing federal law is now verboten and releasing violent criminals is now encouraged. If you think that was a blue in November I have a million Aeroplan points valued at 2.05 cents a piece.

These THUGs need to go back to jail and not pre-tend to be police. Hopefully, the recent blue wave will be the first step in returning the United States to respect all people, since "All PEOPLE are created equal" and Project 2025 is NOT our Constitution. Your attempt at turning the US into Russia West has failed, time to retake our country! ICE OUT

Governor Ferguson went further than this article notes: he is calling for disbanding ICE entirely. I concur with that opinion. ICE has become a police agency that routinely violates more laws than it enforces. It's time that ICE, as an agency (not the agents) gets the death penalty. From a common sense perspective--whose bright idea was it to make arrests in a crowded jetway while active boarding was going on? I would hope those agents are suspended without pay while this is thoroughly investigated and eventually fired for lack of judgment, but I am not holding my breath. From a fiscally conservative point of view--ICE is a huge, money wasting bureaucracy that we don't need. From a historical point of view--Let us not forget that ICE is a relatively new agency. It arose from the hysteria following 9/11, and much like the supposed WMDs in Iraq were used as an excuse to attack Iraq, ICE's creation was based on a lie. The 9/11 hijackers were all properly documented, had valid visas to be in the USA, and made a point of using their real identities. Had ICE existed prior to 9/11, it would have done nothing at all to prevent the attacks. Being against ICE is not the same thing as being against all immigration enforcement. Before ICE, we had enforcement: after ICE, we will still have enforcement but it will be appropriate. From a civil rights point of view--ICE continues to violate the rights of US citizens and legal residents on a routine basis. If they can do that to one legal resident, they can do it to ANY legal resident. If you approve of ICE now, you might want to consider what might happen if ICE still exists when a new president takes office. And, if you are on this forum, you likely travel elsewhere in the world. What goes around comes around, i.e., I would like to continue to be treated fairly outside the USA.

In recent years, first-class, business-class and premium economy have stolen many of the headlines when it comes to air travel — and there’s a big reason for that.

Airlines have leaned heavily into premium seating, with the fancy suites and recliners serving as the biggest money-makers on the plane.

That has led to a ton of luxe new suites and features, like United's Polaris Studios which debuted earlier this year with 27-inch screens.

At the same time, we’re also seeing some intriguing new innovations in economy, too.

To be clear, the seats aren’t suddenly getting wider, and the legroom isn’t magically improving.

But a growing number of airlines are rolling out some new options and upgrades that should ultimately lead to more enjoyable flights, without the need to pay thousands of dollars (or hundreds of thousands of points).

For starters, there’s the Wi-Fi. It has long been a pain point for travelers, as they'd be stuck paying a fee for an often-spotty service.

Nearly all of the large U.S. carriers now offer — or have plans to offer — on-board internet free to members of their loyalty programs.

Most U.S. airlines are installing or preparing to install ultrafast service from Starlink, which is widely regarded as the fastest Wi-Fi in the sky today.

The days of being disconnected when you fly are fast disappearing.

Whenever I sleep on a red-eye flight in coach, I tend to wake up with a sore neck.

This year, Emirates debuted a new feature that should help.

Its "U-Dream" setup has side wings that cradle your neck as you sleep. You can see what it looks like below.

Swipe to see me trying out a "generic" version of the concept at an aviation conference last year.

If you're going to be in economy, that headrest looks like it would definitely make the experience more comfortable — especially on a long flight from the U.S. to Dubai.

Walk-up snack bars are popping up on some commercial planes, which double as a way to stretch your legs during a long flight — and get some sustenance at 35,000 feet.

United used the last row of its new Airbus A321XLR for a snack bar, which will be a nice option for passengers flying that single-aisle plane on long-haul routes.

A handful of additional U.S. carriers have announced plans to offer their snack bars in the sky in the near future. JetBlue has offered a snack "pantry" for years on its long-range planes.

Don’t want to splurge on a pricey business-class or premium economy seat?

United recently announced it would join Air New Zealand in offering a couch, of sorts, in economy.

Next year, the carrier plans to debut a product it’s calling its “Relax Row” on some long-haul flights.

Available as a paid add-on, the concept allows you to turn three economy seats into one "bed." The airline has framed this as a strong option for families traveling together.

The setup is similar to the “Skycouch" Air New Zealand has offered on its long transpacific flights for years.

United plans to outfit some of its largest twin-aisle jets with the “Relax Row,” including some Boeing 777 and 787 aircraft.

How much would you pay for a few hours of shut-eye?

Air New Zealand plans to one-up itself soon with a new bunk-bed in coach.

The new “Skynest” concept will feature two sets of bunk beds stacked three high, with a ladder to reach the upper bunks.

Passengers will be able to book a four-hour nap for an additional fee of $495.

It’s not business-class, but if your only goal is to get some sleep on a long flight from the U.S. to New Zealand, it could be well worth it.

Speaking of ultra-long journeys, Qantas is preparing to launch the world’s longest flights.

Its “Project Sunrise” service from Sydney to London is scheduled to start in October 2027. The service will be followed by flights from Sydney to New York City.

On board the ultra-long-range Airbus A350-1000, passengers won’t just find new premium seating options.

There will also be a “well-being zone,” where passengers can walk around, stretch — and maybe even do a few exercises.

That movement is crucial on flights that will span nearly a full day in the air.

Meanwhile, even as passengers board with multiple screens and devices in their bags, airlines are doubling down on seatback screens.

In the U.S., they’re already a staple on United, Delta Air Lines and JetBlue.

But carriers are also upgrading their seatback entertainment with better headphone technology, streaming services and entertainment options.

United has been working to equip all of its seatback devices with Bluetooth pairing technology, which allows passengers to connect their Apple AirPods and similar devices to the screens.

The carrier also recently rolled out a new partnership with Spotify, which lets flyers stream from their accounts on the seatback screen.

Delta, meanwhile, has launched a seatback partnership with YouTube — and is preparing to deploy new, next-generation screens with a host of new inflight features.

As all of that unfolds, American is pivoting back to screens after removing them from its planes years ago. It will be some time before they are widely available, though.

Airlines have also struck up content partnerships with major newspapers (like the Delta-Wall Street Journal tie-up) and streaming platforms (like United’s with Apple TV+).

We’ve come a long way from the days when the whole plane would watch the same movie on communal screens.

#6065. Southwest Airlines' New 6-Hour Alaska Route Is Flopping: Here's Why

Southwest Airlines has not flown to Alaska for long. The increasingly evolving hybrid operator's first service to the Last Frontier was on May 15, 2026. Two routes were available from the get-go, with flights from Las Vegas and Denver, both of which are major cities for Southwest.

Many routes take time to develop, while some perform worse than anticipated despite strong enough expectations. An airline will often be able to tell how well a new link will do within the first couple of days of tickets going on sale. Initial data for Southwest's two markets suggests that one, in particular, might not be doing particularly well.

It is important to note that data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT) is currently only available until the end of August 2026, although that was only half-a-month before the first season's flights from Las Vegas and Anchorage ended. As it does not consider the full season, it is not fully comprehensive and is, therefore, perhaps somewhat unfair, especially given Alaska is a brand-new state for the airline. Treat it for what it is: a simple snapshot of initial performance.

Covering 2,002 nautical miles (3,708 km) each way, Southwest ran daily between Las Vegas and Anchorage in the first season. The DOT shows that 26,097 round-trip passengers were transported between May and August. However, the load factor was only 68.7%. That was over ten percentage points lower than the carrier's average load at Las Vegas in the same period.

This is just one part of the pie. What about fares? Cirium's Route Grader Report is currently only available until June 2026, so data provides even less of a view. In the first month-and-a-half of life, this new route had an average fare that was 17% higher than the airline's overall network from Las Vegas, but the distance was virtually double the length.

When this imbalance is considered, the new route to Alaska had distance-adjusted total revenue per available seat mile of 9.23 US cents, which was by far Southwest's worst result from Sin City. More than just this, it was the airline's fourth-lowest result across its entire network.

Despite only limited initial data, the DOT indicates that just under a quarter of Southwest's traffic only flew between Las Vegas and Anchorage. They did not fly elsewhere. Despite the carrier's daily service and 'relatively' low fares, it only captured 11% of the local market. In contrast, Alaska Airlines had 79% of it.

Southwest was massively reliant on those who connected to another flight at Nevada's busiest airport. The overnight service from Anchorage, leaving just before midnight and arriving at about 6:00 AM, is designed for that transfer traffic. Despite this and Southwest's considerable network from Sin City, the early overall load was not good (68.7%).

The low result was perhaps influenced by launching two routes to Alaska simultaneously, both of which have a similar schedule and both of which focus on connectivity. Analysis shows that the top ten markets from Anchorage via Las Vegas were Dallas Love, Phoenix, Austin, San Antonio, Sacramento, Salt Lake City, San Diego, Orlando, Ontario, and Albuquerque.

The US will have 44% fewer flights next Thursday, leading to lots of temporary changes. Find out more inside!

In 2026, Southwest operated nonstop between May 15 and September 14, with 123 round-trip flights available. In 2027, the first departure of the season will now be on June 3, three weeks later. The final service of the year will be on September 13. In total, 103 movements will exist, down by 16% year-over-year.

What is more notable is that the equipment has changed, although it is possible that it'll change again. For now, at least, the 175-seat 737 MAX 8 has been replaced by the 137-seat 737-700, contributing to a 34% reduction in seats for sale. Perhaps the MAX 7 will take over. The downgauge means that 14,000+ seats have been removed. Clearly, Southwest is taking big action to achieve stronger fare, yield, and load factor performance next year.

#6063. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

There’s no activity required to earn the 10,000 bonus miles in your AAdvantage Business account. Let me emphasize that with AAdvantage Business, miles are accrued to the business, and can then be shared with any company member, so they can redeem through their personal AAdvantage account.

There’s one main catch with the AAdvantage Business program, which is that in order to actually redeem the rewards you earn, you need to meet one of two activity requirements:

There are many reasons to apply for the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, and the unique double dipping opportunity cardmembers are eligible for, which has made this one of my go-to cards for everyday spending.

The AAdvantage Business program is offering 10,000 bonus miles to new businesses that sign-up with promotion code BNS10K. Assuming you’re eligible, this is absolutely worth taking advantage of.

The only catch is that in order to actually cash out those miles from your business account, you need to have qualifying activity. #6061. The Billion-Dollar Companies Behind Half Of The World's Commercial Aircraft

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

While household names such as United Airlines and Lufthansa dominate the skies in terms of fleet count, there are many companies in existence that have similarly sized fleets that do not carry passengers or cargo, nor do they operate charter missions. These companies never sell a ticket, operate a route, or pursue significant branding campaigns.

Some of these firms control fleets worth tens of billions of dollars, and one owns more aircraft than many of the airlines the public recognizes. The airline industry is composed primarily of two main financial systems: ownership and lease.

Many companies such as Delta Air Lines are known for owning a high percentage of their fleet, notably their older Boeing 717 or Boeing 767 fleets. However, the majority of airlines lease a portion of their jets, as many aircraft with long order backlogs at the manufacturer itself can be hard to obtain. Leasing is a common way to bypass delivery delays.

Most people assume airlines buy the aircraft they fly. Increasingly, that is not the case. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), leasing now accounts for more than half of the world's commercial fleet, making aircraft leasing one of the most important yet least visible sectors in aviation.

Rather than purchasing aircraft outright, many airlines rent them under long-term agreements from specialized leasing companies. The scale of those firms is difficult to appreciate until their fleets are examined. AerCap, the world's largest aircraft lessor, reported owning 1,501 aircraft and managing another 148 at the end of 2025, with an additional 283 aircraft on order.

Those figures make AerCap a larger aircraft owner than many of the world's biggest airlines. Meanwhile, competitors such as SMBC Aviation Capital, Avolon, BOC Aviation, and Air Lease Corporation collectively control thousands more aircraft worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

However, ownership and operation are not the same thing. If airlines do not own many of the aircraft they fly, why would they willingly hand that responsibility to someone else? While there are many sides to the discussion, the answer relates to the complexities of operating an airplane to begin with, which is far more involved than car or boat ownership, for example.

A new Boeing 787-9 carries a list price exceeding $300 million, while even narrowbody aircraft represent investments worth tens of millions of dollars each. Purchasing hundreds of aircraft outright would require enormous amounts of capital that airlines often prefer to dedicate elsewhere. Dry leasing is the most common and most cost-effective way to accomplish this cost benefit.

Aircraft leasing allows airlines to expand fleets without making the full upfront purchase themselves. Instead, leasing firms acquire aircraft from manufacturers such as Boeing and Airbus and lease them to airlines over periods that frequently range from six to twelve years. Airlines gain access to modern aircraft while preserving cash and reducing financial risk.

Hundreds of owned and investor-serviced aircraft

Hundreds of owned aircraft and major order book

While having direct operating authority of 1,066 aircraft, United Airlines' fleet also includes a subsection of leased aircraft, according to the SEC. This figure comprises 958 owned and 108 leased, at the end of 2025. This number is significantly less than AerCap's total number of active leases, which, on paper, causes AerCap to resemble a major international airline.

Four leasing companies own thousands of the aircraft that airlines fly every day. Here is how large their fleets are and how they got there.

In practice, passengers rarely notice that a different company owns the aircraft they are flying on. Under a dry lease, the lessor provides the aircraft while the airline supplies its own pilots, maintenance program, insurance, and operating certificates. To passengers, the aircraft appears no different from any other jet in the airline's fleet.

One recent example comes from Avolon's reported October 2025 sale-and-leaseback agreement with TAAG Angola Airlines involving 787-9 aircraft. In that arrangement, the aircraft are operated by TAAG, but ownership remains with the leasing company. Similar transactions occur throughout the industry and frequently involve new aircraft deliveries from Boeing and Airbus. An aircraft may spend its entire operational life flying for airlines that never technically own it.

A wet lease is an entirely different form of leasing, provided by companies like Heston Airlines, Hi Fly, or Wamos Air. The aircraft is frequently in the livery of the lessor, although not always. Further, the in-flight service, cabin crew, and standards are all those of the lessor company. Wet leases generally have a higher cost than dry leases, and are generally shorter in term.

The influence of lessors extends far beyond simple ownership. Because companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital place enormous aircraft orders, they have become some of Boeing's and Airbus' most important customers. Lessors routinely order aircraft years before identifying the airlines that will eventually operate them.

This purchasing power became especially significant during recent supply chain constraints. CAPA reports that aircraft shortages and production delays have strengthened lessors' market positions by increasing aircraft values and lease rates. Airlines seeking growth often cannot wait years for new direct deliveries, making leased aircraft one of the few available solutions.

The result is that lessors frequently influence what aircraft manufacturers build, how quickly airlines can expand, and even which carriers gain access to modern fleets. A major leasing company may place an order measured in hundreds of aircraft, a scale that rivals the purchasing power of many national airlines.

Orders placed by airlines themselves to manufacturers such as Boeing or Airbus are typically more noteworthy. They represent a larger upfront financial commitment and a known destination for production aircraft. Orders placed by lessors are less noteworthy, but still significant from an operational standpoint.

While the end user of the aircraft is not known when, for example, AerCap placed an order for 100 Airbus jets, such an order boosts the inventory of a lessor. This not only provides options for customers, but an entirely different, and at times, more accessible way of expanding a fleet.

Leasing an aircraft engine is expensive, especially in today's industry.

The growing importance of lessors is increasingly tied to aircraft scarcity. Airbus and Boeing continue to work through substantial backlogs measured in thousands of aircraft. For airlines needing capacity sooner rather than later, leasing companies often represent the fastest available path to fleet growth.

Leasing companies also offer smaller airlines and startup carriers alike a lower barrier to entry to operation than buying an aircraft outright from the producer. AerCap provides one of the clearest examples. The company website published an order book of 283 aircraft entering 2026 while simultaneously managing thousands of aviation assets, including engines and helicopters.

That position effectively allows it to act as a bridge between manufacturers producing aircraft and airlines seeking them. Manufacturers in the aviation industry have the greatest amount of market control for their product. However, some of that power can be relinquished when a customer also acts as a distributor. The relationship between the manufacturer and the lessor creates an unusual balance of power.

Manufacturers remain responsible for designing and producing aircraft, but the largest lessors have amassed order books so large that they have become some of Airbus' and Boeing's most important customers. Companies such as AerCap regularly place orders measured in the hundreds of aircraft, allowing them to negotiate from a position of strength while shaping fleet decisions across dozens of airlines simultaneously.

The future significance of aircraft lessors will likely depend on one simple metric: access to aircraft. Airlines can only grow as quickly as new aircraft become available, and both Airbus and Boeing continue to hold order backlogs extending years into the future. Major aircraft manufacturers, while experiencing high backlogs of orders and record customer interest, can lose control of the end use of their product when lessors place massive orders.

That reality places unusual attention on companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital. Their order books, delivery positions, and financing capabilities may determine which airlines can launch new routes, replace aging fleets, or enter emerging markets first.

In an industry built around aircraft availability, the companies holding the keys to future deliveries may become as important as the carriers operating them. The next major test will come as manufacturers work through production constraints and thousands of aircraft currently sitting in order backlogs move toward delivery.

Whether airlines continue shifting toward leased fleets or return to greater ownership could depend on how effectively Boeing and Airbus satisfy demand over the remainder of the decade. For passengers, the aircraft parked at the gate will probably continue wearing airline colors. The more interesting question is whether the real power behind those fleets increasingly belongs to companies whose names never appear on the boarding pass.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6060. Rakuten New Member Bonus: $50 Referral Offer & How To Maximize It

Rakuten is my favorite online shopping portal, and if you’re not using it, you’re leaving rewards on the table. Through December 31, 2026, if you join Rakuten through a qualifying referral link and spend $50 within the first 90 days, you’ll receive a $50 bonus. The person referring you can also receive $50. This is even an opportunity to earn Amex Membership Rewards points or Bilt Points at a very favorable ratio.

Taking advantage of this Rakuten sign-up bonus is truly a no-brainer, as I’d view this as a way to get $50 worth of stuff for (basically) free. For that matter, you’re missing out more broadly if you’re not earning additional rewards for your online shopping, beyond what you earn with your credit card.

In this post I’d like to go over all the details of Rakuten, including how the Rakuten referral bonus works, and the easiest way to maximize it (as it’s really easy to take advantage of, even if you don’t think you have an immediate purchase in mind).

Link: Sign-up for a Rakuten account with a best-ever $50 bonus

Rakuten is a free online shopping and rewards platform that pays users either cash back or points for the shopping they do online. Rakuten partners with over 3,500 online retailers, many of which are well known, ranging from Lowe’s, to Nike, to Target. The Rakuten shopping portal concept is simple — if you click through from Rakuten to the partner website, Rakuten tracks the purchase and gets paid a commission, and then you get a reward as well.

Note that as a consumer, Rakuten is free to use. The commission is paid by the business, so you’ll pay the same price you’d pay if you just went directly to the retailer’s website. To maximize your savings, you can even download the Rakuten browser extension, which will automatically notify you when you can earn extra rewards.

I should mention that there are several online shopping portals out there to choose from, so Rakuten isn’t the only one. Personally I find that Rakuten is my favorite because it has among the largest selection of partners, it gives you the flexibility to earn cash back or points, and I also find the earnings rates to be very competitive.

It can always pay to use a site like Cashback Monitor to compare the earnings rates for retailers across portals, so that you’re maximizing your rewards. In some situations you may be better off using other portals, so it’s always worth understanding what your options are.

Through December 31, 2026, Rakuten is offering a generous elevated refer-a-friend bonus. Specifically, if you refer a friend to Rakuten and they spend $50 within the first 90 days, then both the person referring and the person being referred each receive $50.

This is truly a best-ever bonus, as we’ve previously only seen a bonus of up to $40 — though admittedly this offer has stuck around for quite some time.

This is a very good deal. Essentially Rakuten is giving out $100 total for a $50 purchase, between the person referring and the person being referred. Long term you can potentially get even more value with Rakuten, as rewards can be converted into Amex or Bilt Points.

Actually earning the $50 Rakuten sign-up bonus is really straightforward:

What’s the timeline with which you’ll actually receive the rewards? With Rakuten you’re paid (either in cash or points) once quarterly, and there’s a cutoff for payments, per the below chart.

Rakuten partners with literally thousands of retailers, and an eligible purchase worth at least $50 with any eligible retail partner would qualify. When you click over to the partner site, just make sure you keep an eye on any exclusions, since some types of purchases may not qualify for rewards.

There are also often amazing opportunities to earn up to 100% back or 100x points with select retailers, which is a rate at which I’d gladly buy points all day long, without even factoring in the service being sold. So I take advantage of these deals all the time, even if I don’t actually value the product.

If you’re not interested in that and don’t have anything you need to buy right now, there’s another creative option. There are easy ways to unlock the $50 bonus, including simply purchasing a $50 gift card through giftcards.com. This is so easy — you can pick up a $50 gift card with a variety of retailers, and then you’ll receive $50 in cash.

To briefly explain that process, you’d enter giftcards.com in the search bar at the top of Rakuten’s website.

Then click the “Shop Now” button, which will take you to giftcards.com. All your purchases while on that site will automatically be tracked.

The website sells a variety of gift cards with popular retailers, including DoorDash, Uber, Delta, Southwest, Hulu, Netflix, Dominos, and many more.

For example, you could buy a $50 DoorDash gift card at face value, and the code will be delivered by email within minutes.

Once the purchase is complete, you should see Rakuten automatically tracking the purchase.

Within an hour the purchase should be fully reflected — the Rakuten account will show a credit in the amount of the sign-up bonus, plus the rewards for the actual purchase (which will vary based on whether you choose to earn cash or points). As a standard, giftcards.com offers either 1% cash back, or one point per dollar spent, but sometimes we see increased offers (like right now).

Taking advantage of this is the obvious choice, in my opinion:

The reason that Rakuten is my favorite shopping portal is because Rakuten rewards can be converted into Amex Membership Rewards points or Bilt Rewards points. The exact way this works depends on the currency you choose to earn.

With the Rakuten and Amex Membership Rewards partnership, you can consistently earn one point in lieu of one cent, assuming you have an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards points. So if a retailer offers 10% cash back, you can instead earn 10x Amex points.

Based on my latest points valuations, Amex Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, because of all the ways there are to redeem the points for first and business class international travel, while getting outsized value. To me that increases the value of the rewards by 70%.

This just requires changing one setting in your account, so it’s super easy. The only thing to be aware of is that this points earning opportunity doesn’t apply to the welcome bonus, but does apply to all spending beyond that.

That’s not the only opportunity, though. The Rakuten and Bilt Rewards partnership lets members earn Bilt Rewards points in lieu of cash back. Bilt elite members can earn one point in lieu of every one cent, while non-elite members can earn one point in lieu of every two cents. Much like Amex Membership Rewards points, I also value Bilt Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, as there are also many good uses of this points currency.

What’s cool here is that your cash back can retroactively be converted into Bilt Points for the entire Rakuten “payout” period (roughly quarterly), and that means even the refer-a-friend bonus can be converted into points.

If you have the choice between one Amex point or one Bilt point, I think many people might prefer the latter, given the value of the rewards, plus how hard they are to earn. However, if the ratio isn’t one point per cent, then I’d go with the Amex partnership instead.

Beyond the rewards you earn directly with Rakuten, your spending with retailers can of course also earn credit card rewards.

Rakuten’s co-branded Amex card is among the best cards for Rakuten spending, as it earns 4% cash back on those purchases, on up to $10,000 per calendar year. Beyond that, purchases with online retailers typically don’t qualify for any exciting bonus categories, so most consumers will want to use one of the best cards for everyday spending.

For business cards, The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more) and Capital One Venture X Business (learn more) are among the best.

Of course there are exceptions, since Rakuten also partners with some brands that may be in categories eligible for bonus rewards on some cards. There are a couple more Rakuten tips I should mention:

Once you join Rakuten, you too can then refer friends and family members, and earn an unlimited number of referral bonuses. Finding your link is easy. Just log into your Rakuten account, and then click on the “Refer & Earn” button at the top left. Then you can either email them an invitation, or you can just send them the URL, and they can apply through that.

Since only a $50 purchase is required for the Rakuten referral bonus, that’s like getting $50 worth of stuff more or less for free. When you're applying for a credit card, you may wonder: "How good is the welcome offer I'm applying for?"

There's no simple answer to this question, but knowing the previous offers a card has had can help you determine what constitutes a good welcome offer. Getting any welcome offer is better than getting nothing at all, but you wouldn't want to apply for a card only to see a better offer a month later.

Generally, you’ll want good to excellent credit to qualify for many of the Capital One cards on this list, though other factors can also affect your approval odds.

We’ve collected and analyzed the offer history over the past few years for Capital One's most popular cards and determined the best time to apply for each.

Limited-time offer on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Earn more than $1,000 in travel bonuses with a limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, plus earn 75,000 bonus miles once you spend $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

It's important to note that we'll only discuss publicly available welcome offers. However, you might receive targeted offers that offer more bonus miles or cash back. You can also check for preapproved Capital One offers without affecting your credit score, which may help you find targeted offers that are higher than the publicly available bonus.

Keep in mind that offers may change at any time, and some of those mentioned below may not be available.

The bonus offer values throughout this guide are based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and are not provided by the credit card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card earns an unlimited 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, plus 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, rental cars and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel.

The card’s modest $95 annual fee, simple earning structure and solid return on everyday spending make it a keeper once you’re approved for it.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture Rewards:

Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening (public offer).

The highest offer we've seen on this card allowed new cardholders to earn up to 100,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offers more than 75,000 miles — whether through additional miles or a travel credit — it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One Venture Business card is a straightforward option for business owners who want consistent travel rewards without having to track bonus categories. With a $95 annual fee, it offers simple earning rates, easy-to-use credits and flexible redemption options that help offset the cost year after year.

While it doesn’t come with premium perks like lounge access, its simplicity and solid earning structure make it a reliable long-term choice for everyday business spending.

The Venture Business's launch offer of up to 150,000 miles (75,000 miles after spending $7,500 on purchases in the first three months, plus an additional 75,000 miles after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months) is the best offer we've seen so far.

As a recently launched card, the Venture Business has only two bonus offers. Since there’s limited historical data, we recommend applying when the bonus is over 100,000 miles.

With plentiful, easy-to-understand perks, the Capital One Venture X is a no-brainer for all travelers, from luxury seekers to the more budget-minded, and the card practically pays for itself year after year.

Though the card carries a $395 annual fee, it offers a $300 annual credit toward bookings made through Capital One Travel and rewards cardholders with 10,000 bonus miles each account anniversary.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture X:

The highest offer we've seen on this card offered 100,000 bonus miles earned after spending $10,000 on purchases within the first six months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is 75,000 miles or higher, it's a good time to apply.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

The Venture X Business carries the same $395 annual fee as the personal version and offers the same major perks, including a $300 annual travel credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel and access to Capital One and participating Priority Pass lounges. It also carries the same earning rates as the Venture X.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture X Business:

The highest offer we've seen on this card is up to 400,000 bonus miles: Earn 200,000 miles after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus an additional 200,000 miles after spending $150,000 on purchases in the first six months.

When the bonus offer is for more than 150,000 miles, it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

While it comes with fewer perks, the Capital One VentureOne Rewards offers the same great redemption options as its sister cards, the Capital One Venture Rewards and the Capital One Venture X, with no annual fee. You’ll earn a flat 1.25 miles per dollar spent on everyday purchases.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One VentureOne Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen allowed new cardholders to earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 in the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offers more than 20,000 miles — whether through additional miles or a travel credit — it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card

The biggest downsides to cash-back cards are low earning rates and a lack of bonus categories, but that’s definitely not true of the Capital One Savor Cash Rewards.

For no annual fee, the Savor offers strong cash-back earning rates on popular and often overlooked categories, including 3% back on dining, entertainment and popular streaming services.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Savor Cash Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen included a $100 Capital One Travel credit to use in the first year. Plus, new cardholders could receive a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is $250 or more, it meets our criteria for applying.

The Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards is another great card with no annual fee. It earns a reliable 1.5% cash back on all purchases, making it a perfect go-to card for the odd purchase that doesn’t fit in any bonus categories.

While many other cards offer higher earning potential in specific spending categories, this card offers the safety of knowing you’ll earn a solid 1.5% back no matter what you buy.

The card has a modest $150 annual fee that can be refunded after spending at least $150,000 in your card anniversary year.

When the bonus is $2,000 or higher, it meets our application criteria.

The Capital One Spark Cash earns 5% cash back on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel and 2% cash back on all other purchases. With the flat rate earning structure, the card is ideal for businesses with spending across different categories.

The Spark Cash is a traditional credit card that allows cardholders to carry a balance, offering more flexibility for businesses that don’t want to pay their balance in full each month.

The Capital One Spark Cash Select is a solid option for small-business owners who want to earn straightforward cash-back rewards without paying an annual fee.

When the bonus exceeds $500, it meets our application threshold.

#6058. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6057. Air New Zealand Denied All Slots For New 27-Hour Route: Here's Why

Air New Zealand has been looking to return to the UK market for some time. The last time we saw its black-and-white livery was in March 2020, when it operated its final flight from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) to Auckland International Airport (AKL). Since then, passengers traveling between the UK and New Zealand have had to rely on connecting flights through hubs in the Middle East, Asia or Australia.

That being said, for the upcoming summer 2027 season, the New Zealand flag carrier had sought to secure slots at Heathrow. According to Airport Coordination Limited's (ACL) Initial Coordination Report for London Heathrow, the Star Alliance member requested 434 slots for the season. However, none of these were approved.

Air New Zealand had been flying to London for several decades. The airline initially served London Gatwick Airport (LGW) from Auckland, with stops in Papeete, Tahiti, and Los Angeles. In 1994, it moved its operations to Heathrow, where it continued to fly via Los Angeles. Between 2006 and 2013, the airline also offered flights via Hong Kong.

However, the Star Alliance member eventually decided to discontinue its London service due to low passenger numbers. It is unclear what routing it would have used had it secured the slots for summer 2027. Los Angeles appears to have been one possibility, as a spokesperson previously told Simple Flying that the airline would most likely operate the service via the US city using Boeing 777 aircraft.

Interestingly, Air New Zealand had also applied for slots at London Gatwick for the previous summer season and was actually successful in securing them. However, the airline never launched the flights, as it was facing aircraft availability issues at the time. Up to four of its 14 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners were grounded simultaneously due to problems with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines and maintenance delays.

These aircraft have since returned to service. Nevertheless, aircraft availability remains a concern. According to ch-aviation, Air New Zealand currently has nine 777-300ERs and 16 787-9s, although only 11 of the latter are in active service. The airline is also awaiting deliveries of three additional 787-9s and five 787-10s, with its outstanding Dreamliner orders expected to be fulfilled by 2028.

However, Boeing has faced difficulties increasing 787 production to its target of ten aircraft per month, partly due to supply-chain delays involving General Electric GEnx engines. These issues have affected deliveries to customers, including Air New Zealand, although planespotters.net data shows that the airline received two Dreamliners in October 2026.

Apart from new aircraft deliveries, the Star Alliance member is also refurbishing its existing widebody fleet. As of late October, 13 of its 14 787-9s had completed cabin upgrades, which include replacing the older inward-facing Business Premier seats with private suites, updating Economy cabins and introducing bunk-style sleeping pods on selected aircraft.

The final Dreamliner is expected to return to service before the end of the year. The airline is also scheduled to begin refurbishing its 777 fleet in March 2027. All of which are expected to undergo the upgrades by the end of 2027, meaning aircraft will need to be temporarily withdrawn from service while the work takes place.

Air New Zealand is one of the principal airlines operating in the South Pacific, with a fleet for NZ's domestic needs and ultra-long-haul routes.

The exact reason why Air New Zealand did not receive any slots has not been confirmed. However, Heathrow is one of the most slot-constrained airports in the world, and securing additional slots is difficult. According to ACL's report, airlines requested a total of 26,832 slots for summer 2027, but only 151 were allocated, just 0.6% of the requests.

Xiamen Air, which recently launched a weekly service between Xiamen and Heathrow, received most of the approved slots. However, several other airlines were unsuccessful. These included Alaska Airlines, which only began flying to Heathrow from Seattle in May and requested 434 slots for next summer. Emirates also failed to secure any of the 1,920 slots it requested, while Virgin Atlantic, Delta Air Lines, Air India and Riyadh Air were denied all 1,798, 556, 1,736 and 868 slots they sought, respectively.

#6056. Alaska Atmos Rewards Business Card Review: 90K Points & Strong Perks

The Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card is the business credit card of Atmos Rewards, which is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The card is issued by Bank of America, and is a rebranding of the former Alaska Airlines Visa Business Card.

The card has just undergone a full refresh, and there are many reasons to consider picking up this card, especially if you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency. This post is my in-depth Atmos Rewards Business Card review, so I’d like to take a look at the card’s value proposition, for anyone who may be considering applying.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card

Before I get into my Atmos Rewards Business Card review, here’s a brief summary of the key details of the card:

Below are what I consider to be the pros and cons of the Atmos Rewards Business Card.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is the only business card in the Atmos Rewards ecosystem. To start, let’s cover the welcome bonus, card eligibility rules, annual fee, and more, since these are important factors that cardmembers consider.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you’ll get 90,000 bonus points after you make $6,000 or more in purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account. This is the best publicly available bonus that we’ve ever seen on the card, and you can find the bonus offer history in this post.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Atmos Rewards points are worth 1.5 cents each, given the great uses of these rewards. That means the 90,000 points are worth $1,350 for me.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is issued by Bank of America. The good news is that eligibility for this card is unrelated to having any other Atmos Rewards card, so you’re eligible for this card (including the bonus) if you have the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more) or Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more).

Let me emphasize that you are eligible for this product if you have any of the previously issued personal or business HawaiianMiles Barclays cards, or any of the previously issued personal Alaska Mileage Plan cards.

Beyond that, Bank of America doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for business cards. While Bank of America has the 2/3/4 rule and 3/12 rules, those apply to personal cards, and not business cards. Generally those with a Bank of America banking relationship also have the best odds of approval (though it’s by no means a requirement).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to have to be approved for this card, though personally I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

Applying for this card won’t count as a further card toward Chase’s 5/24 limit, in case that’s a limit you’re trying to stay under.

I should also mention the following restriction in the terms:

I also understand that I may be declined for additional credit card accounts if my business entity currently has, or has had, another business card with Bank of America in the preceding 24 month period.

On the surface, this suggests you may be declined for a Bank of America business card if you have another Bank of America business card. However, anecdotally, this doesn’t appear to be enforced much. I think the term “may” is the key here (which is different than “will”).

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has a $195 annual fee. That’s on the steep side, though the card does have some premium perks. The good news is that you can add employee cards at no extra cost, so that annual fee covers the cost for all the cards you’ll have.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has bonus categories that can help you rack up points faster. Furthermore, spending on the card can help you earn Atmos Rewards elite status. Let’s talk about how rewarding spending on the card can be.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 10x points per dollar spent on flights booked through the Atmos for Business website. If you’re looking to maximize your earning, this is where you want to book your Alaska and Hawaiian flights, as this is an incredible deal.

You do need your own business to participate in the Atmos for Business program, and once registered, the return on spending is really tough to beat. Based on my valuation of points, that’s like an incremental 15% return on eligible airfare spending, on top of what you otherwise earn.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 3x points on all other eligible Alaska and Hawaiian purchases, with no caps. Based on my valuation of Atmos Rewards points, that’s like a 4.5% return on spending. So if you fly either of those Alaska Air Group carriers with any frequency, that’s a solid return on that spending.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 2x points on eligible dining purchases. Based on my valuation of Atmos Rewards points, that’s like a 1.5% return on spending. It’s always nice to earn bonus points, though in fairness, 2x points isn’t exactly the biggest return on spending that we’ve seen.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 1x points on all other eligible spending. Based on my valuation of Atmos Rewards points, that’s like a 1.5% return on spending. As you might expect, there are more exciting cards for everyday spending, as independently, that’s not a terribly exciting return.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card can help you earn elite status in the Atmos Rewards program. Specifically, the card offers one status point for every $3 in eligible spending. There’s no cap on how many status points you can earn with the card.

If you are serious about earning status with spending, I’d recommend instead considering the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), which offers one status point for every $2 in eligible spending.

Beyond the ability to earn one status point per $3 spent, the Atmos Rewards Business Card offers some additional threshold bonuses for spending, including bonus status points and discount codes:

In other words, spending $200,000 per anniversary year would earn you 20,000 bonus status points, plus a discount code for 50% off a base fare. Just to cover the basics of that 50% off base fare discount code, here’s how that works:

So the value of this will depend on how you’d usually travel, but this could easily save you many hundreds of dollars, depending on the type of ticket you book. It’s also still possible to upgrade these tickets, but at least the initial booking has to be in economy.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card also offers a Bank of America relationship bonus. If you have an eligible small business Bank of America checking or savings account, you’ll receive a bonus equal to 10% of the points you earn on each dollar spent.

This is a way to earn even more rewards, as you’d earn 11x points on Atmos for Business purchases, 3.3x points on Alaska and Hawaiian purchases, 2.2x points on the other purchases eligible for bonus categories, and 1.1x points on everyday spending.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a decent card to use for purchases abroad, since you can rack up rewards without paying a fee.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers a variety of benefits and credits, which can potentially more than justify the annual fee year after year. These perks are the main reason you want to consider picking up this card, in addition to the great welcome bonus. In no particular order, let’s go over the main benefits.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers a free checked bag for you and up to six guests on the same reservation when flying on Alaska or Hawaiian. In order to be eligible for this perk, you need to charge the cost of the ticket to your card. Another great thing is that authorized users on the card can also receive this benefit, as long as their ticket is purchased with the card, so that’s a huge incentive to add authorized users to the card.

This is a great benefit that could save you a lot of money — Alaska and Hawaiian ordinarily charge $30-45 per checked bag, so that’s a savings of up to $90 per person roundtrip, if checking bags. If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian fairly often but don’t have elite status, that alone could quickly more than justify the annual fee.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers preferred boarding for you and up to six guests on the same reservation. In order to be eligible for this perk, you need to charge the cost of the ticket to your card. Another great thing is that authorized users on the card can also receive this benefit, as long as their ticket is purchased with the card.

This is a valuable benefit that helps you ensure that there’s space in the overhead bin for your bags. It’s also an awesome authorized user perk, so that you can share this benefit with others.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers four Alaska Lounge passes annually. The way this works, the primary cardmember will have one Alaska Lounge pass deposited into their Atmos Rewards account at the beginning of the quarter, valid through the end of the quarter.

Each is valid for access to Alaska Lounges on a single calendar day, in conjunction with a same day flight operated by Alaska, Hawaiian, a oneworld airline, or an Alaska global partner. Each pass is valid for one adult, plus accompanying children. For what it’s worth, a day pass would otherwise cost $60 per person.

If you’re the primary cardmember on the Atmos Rewards Business Card, you can share your Atmos Rewards points with other members at no cost. The way this works, you can link your accounts with up to 10 other Atmos Rewards members (they don’t have to be family — accounts of friends are fine as well), and then you can move points back and forth for free.

I’d argue that this is especially compelling for families, because it’s easier to rack up a sizable balance of points when you can consolidate them into one account.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 20% back on Alaska and Hawaiian inflight purchases when paying with your card. This applies for the purchase of food, beverages, and Wi-Fi onboard flights, and the statement credit should post to your account within seven days. There’s no limit to how often you can take advantage of this.

Let me just mention that Alaska and Hawaiian should have free Starlink Wi-Fi fleetwide by some point in 2027, at which point there won’t be savings anymore with Wi-Fi. That being said, it can still be used for food and beverages.

If you’re the primary cardmember on the Atmos Rewards Business Card, then you’re eligible for a free same day confirmed flight change on Alaska. This ordinarily costs $50 per person, so that’s quite valuable.

With this, you can change to another flight that might be more convenient, subject to capacity controls. This is especially useful in high frequency markets.

If you’re the primary cardmember on the Atmos Rewards Business Card, you’re eligible to receive a $50 voucher if you have an Alaska flight that is delayed by at least two hours, or that’s canceled within 24 hours of departure.

The $50 voucher is valid for 48 hours, and will be delivered to the email address associated with the reservation, and can be used for food, drinks, etc. Travel must have been booked directly with Alaska using the eligible credit card.

Those with the Atmos Rewards Business Card receive up to a $120 airport security credit every four years, in connection with TSA PreCheck or Global Entry. This is a perk offered by many premium credit cards, and there’s lots of value to this.

When talking about an Atmos Rewards credit card, it’s worth acknowledging the general value in earning and redeeming Atmos Rewards points. Alaska & Hawaiian are both in the oneworld alliance, and Atmos Rewards partners not only with oneworld partner airlines, but also with all kinds of other unaligned airlines. I consider Atmos Rewards to be one of the most valuable points currencies out there.

Atmos Rewards has a distance based award chart, which varies a bit by region. For example, below is the one-way award chart within the Americas.

I constantly redeem Atmos Rewards points for travel within the United States, particularly on American. For example, all the time I redeem 4,500 points to fly one-way economy from Miami to Tampa (when cash fares would often be $200+), or 15,000 points to fly one-way business class from Miami to Chicago or New York (when cash fares would often be $500+). You simply can’t beat these redemption rates.

The icing on the cake is that with Atmos Rewards, you earn status points for award flights, so those flights even count toward elite status, and that’s also why I’ve switched my business to Atmos Rewards.

Of course there are lots of other opportunities with Atmos Rewards points as well. For example, I love the ability to redeem 75,000 points for one-way business class from the United States to many parts of Asia on carriers like Japan Airlines or Starlux Airlines — those are both awards that I’ve booked for myself in the past, and they were a great value.

What makes this an even better value is that you can have a free stopover on a one-way award when traveling long haul. One thing worth being aware of is that Atmos Rewards has a $20 per person per direction partner award booking fee. However, that can be waived if you have the Atmos Rewards Summit Card.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is the only business card in the Atmos Rewards ecosystem, so how valuable is this product? A few thoughts…

First of all, I think there’s a lot of merit to picking up this card for the excellent welcome bonus, which includes a lot of points. The card also has significant ongoing benefits. The card also doesn’t count toward the Chase 5/24 limit, which is nice. Given the value of the Atmos Rewards ecosystem, there’s no reason not to pick up this card, if eligible.

What about the long term value proposition of the card, though? If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency and don’t have elite status, the basic perks add up, including a first checked bag free, preferred boarding, a quarterly lounge pass, free points sharing, and more.

However, I’d say there’s also merit to picking up one (or both) of the personal Atmos Rewards cards…

The $395 annual fee Atmos Rewards Summit Card is the most premium Atmos Rewards credit card. While it’s a personal card, I still think it’s worth highlighting, as it’s incredibly lucrative. I’d take it a step further, and say that it’s my favorite airline credit card.

Among other things, the card racks up status points at the fastest rate, the card allows you to earn Global Companion Awards, offers Alaska Lounge passes, enables free points sharing, waives partner award booking fees, offers 3x points on foreign purchases, and much more.

If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency, then getting this card is an absolute no-brainer. As I see it, the anniversary 25K-point Global Companion Award alone basically justifies the annual fee, and that says nothing of all the other amazing perks.

If you’re not set on an Atmos Rewards Business Card but want a dedicated business credit card that’s lucrative, there are some other great options that earn flexible points. Consider these if you want options for redeeming your rewards for more than just on Alaska, Hawaiian, and its partners:

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is an excellent business credit card that offers a massive welcome bonus and strong perks. The limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points will come in handy for cardmembers, and is more than enough reason to get the card.

If you don’t yet have this card and are eligible, I’d highly recommend applying. This is a card that many people don’t have, yet which offers lots of value and a great bonus.
